correctness.rationale: Every proper simple game through five players is generated from its minimal-winning antichain. Two exact Public-Good computations and two exact dominance tests agree throughout. Full player-relabeling canonicalization gives nine violating classes totaling \(460\) labeled games, and each class is checked against an explicit exact weighted representation.

evidence: Freixas and Kurz state that the Public Good index violates local monotonicity and dominance in general.
They prove dominance on uniform complete games and local monotonicity on uniformly weighted games.
They exhibit the four-player weighted game \([3;2,1,1,1]\) as nonuniform but still satisfying Public-Good dominance.
Holler and Napel study local monotonicity directly and supply weighted examples of the known pathology.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These sources decisively establish the general phenomenon and positive subclasses, so novelty cannot rest on finding a five-player counterexample. They do not imply the complete lower-bound exhaustion or the exact quotient census.

originality.rationale: Prior work already establishes that the Public Good index can violate local monotonicity and dominance; that existence statement is not claimed as new. The inspected literature does not state the complete sharp proper-game boundary consisting of zero violations through four players and exactly \(460\) labeled violations in nine five-player isomorphism classes.
residual_risks: An unindexed historical table, thesis appendix, software corpus, or enumeration of small simple games could contain the same five-player census.
The earlier local-monotonicity literature already contains individual weighted counterexamples, so only the sharp lower bound and complete first-layer classification are asserted as original here.
No statement is made about violation frequencies or symmetry classes for six or more players.

value.rationale: Local monotonicity and dominance are central structural tests for whether voting weight and measured power can move in opposite directions. Identifying the exact first proper-game size at which Public Good fails, and classifying every first obstruction into only nine weighted symmetry types, converts a known qualitative pathology into a sharp structural boundary.
